summary:
Percent germination is germinated seeds divided by seeds sown — the number on a seed packet, and the number that decides how much seed to buy. It returns germination, viability (germinated + dormant), seeds needed for 10 000 plants and sowing rate for 1 000 plants/m², and the panel shows all of them at once.

This calculator adds the viability and vigour figures that explain a low result. The arithmetic keeps full precision internally and only rounds what it displays, so the number you copy out is the number the formula produced. Units are stated on every box and in every result, so a figure copied out of a protocol, a datasheet or a chart can be entered without converting it first.

sections.title: The formula behind the Percent Germination
sections.html:
Germination (%) = germinated ÷ sown × 100

The symbols in the formula
SymbolWhat it stands forUnit
germinatedseeds that produced a normal seedlingseeds
sownseeds placed on the testseeds
germinationthe percentage%

sections.title: How do I use the Percent Germination?
sections.html:
Fill the boxes you have numbers for; the calculator decides what it can derive from them.

  1. Enter the values you already have. Every box accepts a decimal point and a minus sign; thousands separators are ignored.
  2. The grey boxes are results: they are worked out from your inputs and cannot be typed into.
  3. Press Calculate. The results fill in together, and from then on they follow every edit you make — there is no page to reload and nothing to submit.

sections.title: A worked example
sections.html:
Take the default values the page opens with: seeds germinated of 88 seeds, seeds sown of 100 seeds, seeds rotted or dead of 5 seeds.

Substituting them into the formula gives germination of 88%, viability (germinated + dormant) of 95%, seeds needed for 10 000 plants of 11,363.64 seeds, sowing rate for 1 000 plants/m² of 1,136.36 seeds/m².

Because the example uses the defaults, you can reproduce it by loading the page and reading the results panel before touching anything.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
Interpretation is a convention, not part of the arithmetic. The usual bands are:

How to read the result
ResultBandWhat it means
above 90%Excellentsow at the planned rate
70 – 90%Acceptableincrease the rate by the shortfall
below 70%Poorcheck storage, seed lot age and test conditions

  • Standard tests count normal seedlings under specified conditions — 20 °C for most vegetables, alternating temperatures for grasses.

  • Dormant seed is viable but not counted as germinated; a tetrazolium test separates dormancy from death.

  • Vigour (how fast and uniformly seedlings emerge) predicts field establishment better than germination percentage alone.

sections.title: What are the common mistakes?
sections.html:
Before blaming the formula, check these — they explain nearly every mismatch:

  • Counting abnormal seedlings as germinated.
  • Testing too few seeds — 100 is the minimum for a useful percentage.
  • Testing freshly harvested seed that is still dormant.

faq.q: How many seeds do I need for a 95% germination rate and 10 000 plants?
Why is field emergence lower than the test result?
faq.a: Soil temperature, crusting, pathogens and sowing depth all reduce it.

faq.q: What does the Percent Germination actually calculate?
faq.a: It returns germination, viability (germinated + dormant), seeds needed for 10 000 plants and sowing rate for 1 000 plants/m². Each one is derived by the formula on this page, so you can check any figure by hand.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — and if you change an input, every result updates with it.

faq.q: Why is the answer different from the one in my protocol?
faq.a: Nearly always a unit or a rounding difference. This calculator works in the units printed next to each box, keeps full precision internally and only rounds for display, so recomputing from the rounded numbers on screen can differ in the last digit.

faq.q: Can I use it with the numbers straight from a datasheet?
faq.a: Yes. Every box states its unit, and nothing is converted behind your back, so a figure copied from a datasheet, a kit insert or a protocol goes in as printed.
